common.pressRun: Press Run to see what this command does.
common.recorded: This is the screen output of a campaign ran on our GPU server.
common.computed: We did not run this exact combination. The numbers below are worked out in your browser from BindCraft2's own defaults, so treat them as an estimate.
common.refused: BindCraft2 refuses this campaign before it starts. It checks the settings first, so a mistake costs you seconds instead of hours.
common.notCapturedYet: We have not captured this run yet.
common.notAffinity: A score is not an affinity. A confident prediction means the model is sure about the pose, not that the binder is tight or specific.

index.title: Designing a binder with BindCraft2
index.intro: BindCraft2 designs a protein that sticks to a target protein you give it. We run can run it on our own GPU server, and this site replays those runs so you can see what each setting does before you spend hours of GPU time on it.
index.oneCommand: There is one ring (er... command) to rule them all: bindcraft design settings.json. Everything you decide goes in the settings.json settings file, which is why most of this site is about the file and not the command to run BindCraft2 itself.
index.funnelTitle: Most design attempts fail, and that is normal
index.funnel: BindCraft2 makes one design attempt at a time, and checks it after every stage. An attempt that is going nowhere is dropped early, so the GPU is not wasted on it. A short campaign might turn four attempts into two designs. A hard target can take hundreds of attempts for a handful.
index.targets: The first is 3EVG, the dengue virus NS5 methyltransferase. We solved that structure here, so we know it well. The second is IL-15 from the Jamaican fruit bat, which is a predicted model rather than a crystal structure.
process.title: How a campaign works
process.intro: A campaign repeats the same loop until it has the designs you asked for. One pass through the loop is one trajectory, which is one attempt at a binder.
process.stage1: First, the design stages. BindCraft2 starts from a random sequence and pushes it downhill with AlphaFold2, changing the binder until the model predicts it folds and sits on the target. This runs in five stages, and the campaign checks the attempt at the end of each one.
process.stage2: Second, the sequence is redesigned. ProteinMPNN reads the backbone the design stages produced and writes new sequences for it, because the sequence AlphaFold2 hallucinated is usually not the best one for that shape.
process.stage3: Third, each candidate sequence is predicted again from scratch, with models that were held back from the design stages. This is the honest test. A design that only looks good to the models that made it does not count.
process.stage4: Finally, the candidates that pass every filter are ranked, best first.
process.stages: The step counts below are the defaults. Each stage has a confidence floor, and an attempt that falls below the floor is dropped there.
process.screen: screen: explore sequences and where the binder sits on the target.
process.refine: refine: settle the amino acid probabilities at each position.
process.anneal: anneal: move toward one definite sequence rather than a blend.
process.mutate: mutate: try single substitutions to see if any improve it.
process.optimism: The numbers you see during the design stages are optimistic, because the design is being pushed to satisfy the model that is scoring it. Therefore we trust the numbers from the re-prediction step, not these.
target.title: Pick the target and the epitope
target.intro: BindCraft2 needs a structure and the chains you care about. You can also name the residues you want the binder to touch, which are called hotspots.
target.unguided: Hotspots are optional. With none given, BindCraft2 reads the whole surface and picks its own site. That is how we ran our first campaigns on 3EVG, so we could see where it chose to bind without us steering it.
target.hotspotRule: If you do name hotspots, name three to six residues that are actually on the surface. A buried residue cannot be touched, and asking for it wastes the campaign.
target.coldspots: Coldspots are the opposite. They are residues you want left alone, and BindCraft2 pushes the binder away from them.
target.prepare: Prepare the structure before you use it. Strip the waters and any ligand you do not want, and keep the assembly that matters biologically.
target.3evg_apo.note: 3EVG with the waters, the five sulfates and the SAH cofactor removed, so only chain A protein is left.
target.3evg_holo.note: 3EVG with the SAH cofactor still in the pocket. Compare this with the stripped version to see what a bound cofactor does to a campaign.
target.ajil15.note: IL-15 from the Jamaican fruit bat, as a predicted model refined by molecular dynamics. Because it is predicted and not solved, the confidence numbers are worth less here than on a crystal structure.
target.hpdl1.note: Human PD-L1, which ships with BindCraft2 and uses the PD-1 interface as its hotspots. We keep it as a warm-up, because it is the target the method was tuned on.
target.exposure: The bars show how exposed each residue is. A residue is counted as exposed when at least a fifth of its surface is reachable by solvent.
settings.title: The settings file
settings.intro: Everything a campaign does is in one JSON file. BindCraft2 builds the final settings out of six layers, and a later layer overwrites an earlier one.
settings.layers: The layers are: BindCraft2's own defaults, an optional core profile, the modality, the properties you switched on, the named target, your campaign file, and anything you passed with --set on the command line.
settings.layerHint: Click a value to see which layer it came from. This matters, because a setting you did not write can still be in force.
settings.weights: The weights_ settings steer the optimisation itself. They are on different scales, so they do not read as percentages of importance. Leave them alone on a first campaign.
settings.stacking: Each property you switch on adds another bar the design has to clear. Therefore stacking several of them makes an accepted design rarer, not better.
run.title: Run the command
run.intro: Type a command and press Run. Where we have a recorded campaign that matches, you get its real screen output. Where we do not, we work out what would change and say so.
run.subcommands: The other subcommands work on results you already have. rank re-sorts them, filter applies different thresholds, and campaign_output collects the files.
run.resume: A campaign resumes by default. Pointing it at a folder that already holds output, with resume switched off, is refused.
trajectory.title: Watch one attempt
trajectory.intro: This is one trajectory from a real campaign. The target stays still. The binder is built up against it, stage by stage, and the curves on the right are what the optimisation was trying to improve.
trajectory.early: Early on the binder is a vague shape in roughly the wrong place. This is expected. The design is being pulled into shape, not drawn correctly the first time.
trajectory.killed: This attempt was dropped at the {stage} stage, because its {metric} was {value} and the floor is {floor}.
trajectory.survived: This attempt passed every stage check and went on to sequence redesign.
trajectory.contacts: The grid is every binder residue against every target residue. A cell is filled when the two are within four angstroms, which is the same cutoff BindCraft2 uses to count interface residues.
mpnn.title: Redesign the sequence
mpnn.intro: The design stages produce a backbone and a sequence together, but the sequence is usually not the best one for that backbone. ProteinMPNN reads the structure and writes better sequences for the same shape.
mpnn.candidates: BindCraft2 draws up to ten sequences per attempt, stops once three of them pass, and keeps the best one.
mpnn.interface: By default the interface residues are left as the design stages set them, because those are the ones doing the binding.
scoring.title: What the scores mean
scoring.intro: Every number on the ranked table comes from AlphaFold2's own confidence output. This page builds each one from the picture it comes from.
scoring.plddt: pLDDT is per-residue confidence. BindCraft2 writes it into the B-factor column of every structure it saves, on a scale of 0 to 100, so a viewer can colour by it directly.
scoring.unbound: A binder is also predicted on its own, without the target. A design that looks good in the complex and falls apart alone is not a binder, which is why the free binder has its own floor.
scoring.pae: The grid is the predicted aligned error. Each cell is how wrong the model expects to be about one residue when the structure is lined up on another. Low is good.
scoring.ipae: i_pAE is the mean of the interface part of that grid, divided by 31 angstroms. The default ceiling of 0.35 is about 10.85 angstroms, which is the number worth remembering.
scoring.ipdae: i_pDAE is the same idea with the grid masked down to residue pairs within eight angstroms of each other. BindCraft2 ranks designs by it.
scoring.filters: A candidate has to clear every filter. Move a threshold and watch the accepted set change. The table records which filter stopped each candidate, which is the first thing to read when a campaign accepts nothing.
scoring.caveat: None of these numbers is an affinity. A perfect interface score describes a confident predicted pose, not a tight or specific binder. We find out whether a design works at the bench.
ranked.title: Choose which designs to make
ranked.intro: These are the designs that passed every filter, best first. Ordering protein is slow and not free, so the question is which few you would make.
ranked.compare: Pick two designs to see them side by side, with their sequences and their scores.
ranked.desperation: If a campaign runs a long way with nothing accepted, BindCraft2 starts loosening its own settings one step at a time. Designs that came out of that are weaker, and the table marks them.
metric.pLDDT: Per-residue confidence in the binder, in the bound state. Higher is better.
metric.Unbound_Binder_pLDDT: Confidence in the binder predicted on its own, with no target. Higher is better.
metric.Target_pLDDT: Confidence in the target. Mostly a check that the target was read correctly.
metric.pTM: Confidence in the whole complex. Higher is better.
metric.i_pTM: Confidence in the interface itself. Higher is better.
metric.i_pAE: Mean predicted error across the interface, divided by 31 angstroms. Lower is better.
metric.i_pDAE: The interface error with only close contacts counted. This is the ranking score. Higher is better.
metric.Interface_Residues: How many binder residues come within four angstroms of the target.
metric.Interface_BuriedArea: How much binder surface is buried against the target, in square angstroms.
metric.Binder_RMSD: How far the binder moves between its free and bound predictions. Lower means it does not have to change shape to bind.
metric.Backbone_Clashes: Backbone atoms overlapping where they should not. Anything above zero fails.
metric.Binder_Helix_Fraction: The fraction of the binder that is helix.
metric.Binder_BetaSheet_Fraction: The fraction of the binder that is beta sheet.
metric.Binder_Disulfides: Cysteine pairs close enough to form a bond. This is geometry, not a checked bond.
metric.Hotspot_Contact_Fraction: The fraction of the hotspots you named that the binder actually touches.
metric.Coldspot_Contact_Fraction: The fraction of the coldspots the binder touches. Lower is better.
file.ranked: One row per accepted design, best first by i_pDAE.
file.refolded: One row per candidate sequence that was predicted again, with whether it passed and which filters it failed.
file.trajectories: One row per design attempt, including the ones that were dropped.
file.losses: What the optimisation was minimising, per round, for one attempt.
file.metadata: The settings the campaign actually ran with, after all six layers were merged.
target.faces.title: Two faces of the same protein
target.faces.intro: We asked BindCraft2 for binders against bat IL-15 three times, changing only where we pointed it. Face A gave 41 designs. Face B gave none. Both faces are on the surface, both are the same size, and both look reasonable. This is why one of them works.
target.faces.unguided: Look at the unguided campaign first. Nobody told it where to bind. All 41 of its designs landed on Face A, and not one touched a single Face B residue. On average each design contacted 8.8 of the 9 Face A residues and none of the 8 Face B residues. The method had already chosen before we directed it.
target.faces.short: A binder needs something to grip. Face A offers a greasy patch sitting in a dip. Face B is a smooth, wet bulge. That is the whole lesson, and the rest of this section is the measurement behind it.
target.faces.grease: Count only the genuinely water-hating residues, which are Leu, Ile, Val, Phe, Met, Trp, Tyr, Ala and Pro, then measure how much of their surface is really exposed. Face A has more than twice the greasy area per residue, and it has a tyrosine. Face B has no aromatic ring at all.
target.faces.ring: A flat aromatic ring is the most useful thing a designed binder can pack against, because it is large, rigid and gives up almost nothing when it is covered. Face B offers an alanine, which is barely more than a bump, and one isoleucine.
target.faces.greaseWarn: A warning about measuring this. If you simply add up the non-polar surface you will get the wrong answer, because the long arms of Lys, Arg and Glu are non-polar for most of their length. By that bad measure Face B looks better than Face A. Count whole residues by identity instead.
target.faces.shapeTitle: Shape, which is to say somewhere to sit
target.faces.shape: Fit a sphere to each patch and ask which way it curves. The fitted radius is nearly the same for both, about 10 angstroms. The sign is not. Face A curves inward and Face B curves outward.
target.faces.shapeWhy: A dip wraps part way around whatever lands in it, so a binder gets contact on several sides at once. A bulge is the opposite. A binder can only lie on top of it and touch it in one plane.
target.faces.shapeStructure: Why they differ is worth seeing in the structure. Face A spans three different pieces of the fold, a strand edge at Tyr43, then a helix, then a turn. Wherever secondary structure elements meet, the surface has relief, and relief is what makes a groove. Face B is the exposed stripe of two helices lying side by side, and a helix surface is a smooth cylinder.
target.faces.wrongTitle: Three answers that sound right and are wrong
target.faces.wrongScatter: The first is that the hotspots are scattered so no binder can reach them all. That is a real failure mode and worth checking first, but here it is backwards. Face B is one connected patch. Face A comes in two pieces as much as 18.9 angstroms apart, and Face A is the one that works.
target.faces.wrongCharge: The second is that Face B is too charged. Both faces carry a net charge of exactly minus one, and Face A is the more charged surface of the two, with 55 percent of its area on charged residues against 36 percent for Face B.
target.faces.chargePattern: There is a subtler charge story. On Face B the opposite charges sit 5.1 angstroms apart, against 10.5 angstroms on Face A. Face B's acids and bases are already paired with each other, and a charge that has found a partner has nothing left to offer a binder. Look at the pattern, not the total.
target.faces.wrongFloppy: The third is that Face B is a floppy loop. The opposite is true. By DSSP, Face B is 100 percent helix, while Face A is 67 percent helix, 11 percent strand and 22 percent turn. The face that failed is the more rigid and the more regular of the two.
target.faces.funnel: Face B did not produce a poor binder. It produced nothing, and where it stopped is the most useful part of the series. Not one of its 200 attempts reached ProteinMPNN, which means not one of our filters ever ran on a Face B design. There was nothing to filter.
target.faces.funnelStage: Face B attempts were dropped during hallucination, the first half of the method, where a backbone is pushed around until the structure prediction says the two chains are bound. Most died at the anneal stage, and the metric named in the rejection is almost always i_pTM, the model's own confidence that the chains are in contact.
target.faces.funnelNumbers: The median design-stage i_pTM was 0.80 for the unguided run and 0.77 for Face A, against 0.11 for Face B. Face B's whole range is 0.06 to 0.23. That is not a near miss against a bar we set too high. An i_pTM of 0.1 is the model saying there is no interface at all.
target.faces.funnelLesson: This is why the physical measurements matter more than the filter settings. You could lower every threshold in the campaign file to zero and Face B would still give you nothing, because the failure happens before any threshold is consulted.
target.faces.hotspotCost: One more number, because it is a useful surprise. The unguided campaign got 41 designs and the Face A campaign got 27, on the same face. Naming hotspots cost a third of the yield. The unguided run was free to settle on whichever corner came easiest, while the directed run also had to contact half the named residues and stay off the coldspots.
target.faces.checklistTitle: What to look for next time
target.faces.checklist1: Is every residue exposed? A buried residue cannot be touched. The exposure bars above answer this.
target.faces.checklist2: Can one binder reach them? Check the spread. A split set is survivable, a set spread over opposite ends of the protein is not.
target.faces.checklist3: Is there exposed grease, and is there a ring? This is the measurement that predicted both outcomes here. Above about 20 square angstroms per residue is workable, around 10 is marginal, and below 8 is not worth the GPU time. A Tyr, Trp or Phe is worth more than its area suggests.
target.faces.checklist4: Does the surface curve inward anywhere? Prefer a dip, a groove, or the seam where two secondary structure elements meet. Avoid the open face of a lone helix or a pair of them.
target.faces.checklist5: Only then look at charge, and look at the pattern rather than the total. Unpaired charges are an opportunity and self-paired ones are not.
target.faces.closing: The honest summary is that points 3 and 4 did the work here. Points 1, 2 and 5 would all have told you Face B was fine. And once you have chosen a face, name as few hotspots as will do the job, because every residue you name is a constraint the optimiser has to satisfy.
setting.chains: Which chains of the target structure BindCraft2 is allowed to see. Everything else in the file is thrown away before design starts. Leaving an extra chain in gives the binder somewhere else to land, so a design can pass every filter while sitting on the wrong molecule.
setting.hotspots: The target residues you want the binder to touch, written like A43,A58,A62. Naming them steers every trajectory towards that patch instead of letting the model choose. It costs yield: on our IL-15 target the unguided run accepted 41 designs and the directed run on the same face accepted 27, because the directed run also had to satisfy the contact requirement.
setting.coldspots: Target residues the binder must stay off. Useful when a face is already spoken for, by a natural partner or by a site you need to leave free. Coldspots need a real backbone, so a campaign against a sequence rather than a structure is refused.
setting.objective: What the binder is being asked to do with this target. The default is to bind it. Set it to detarget and the optimiser is instead pushed away from that target, which is how you ask for selectivity between two close relatives.
setting.weight: How much this target counts when several are listed. Raising it on one target buys affinity there at the cost of the others. With a single target it does nothing.
setting.target_flexibility: How much the target backbone is allowed to move while the binder is designed. Zero holds it rigid. Raising it makes a shallow or awkward site easier to design against, because the target can open up to meet the binder, and it makes the result less trustworthy, because the real protein may not do that. The desperation ladder raises this to 0.5 on its own when a campaign is failing.
setting.forced_targeting: The lysine trick. During the early gradient stages every exposed target residue outside a shell around your hotspots is mutated to lysine, turning the rest of the surface into a hostile positive patch so the binder has nowhere attractive to sit but your epitope. The real sequence is restored before hardening and validation. It steers where the binder lands, not how tightly it binds, and it needs both a structured target and hotspots.
setting.forced_targeting_shell: The radius in angstroms around your hotspots that forced_targeting leaves alone. The default is 10. A smaller shell squeezes the binder onto a tighter patch. A larger one leaves more of the real surface available and weakens the steering.
setting.modality: What kind of binder to build. The choice loads a preset of lengths, validation model and filters, so it changes far more than its own value. Picking peptide rather than binder, for example, drops the length range from 60 to 180 residues down to 8 to 24.
setting.binder_lengths: The range of binder lengths to draw from, as a low and a high. Each trajectory picks a length inside it. A wider range explores more shapes and spends more time compiling, because BindCraft2 compiles per length bucket. A range outside what your modality supports is refused at start-up.
setting.copies: How many copies of the binder chain to build. More than one asks for an oligomer rather than a single chain, which is what the homo_oligomer modality sets.
setting.aa_bias: Push the sequence towards or away from particular amino acids, as a map like {"C": 0}. Zero does not ban a residue outright, it removes the reward for using it. Setting cysteine to zero is the usual way to avoid unwanted disulfides.
setting.screen_steps: Gradient steps in the first stage, where a backbone is pushed around from noise until the predictor says the two chains are in contact. Cheap steps, and most hopeless attempts die here or just after. Fewer steps screens faster and throws away attempts that might have recovered.
setting.refine_steps: Gradient steps in the second stage, which tidies what screening found. The autotuner adjusts this and screen_steps on its own every ten trajectories unless you turn it off.
setting.anneal_steps: Gradient steps in the stage where the interface has to consolidate into something real. This is where an undesignable epitope stops: on our IL-15 Face B, 151 of the rejections happened here and only 5 of 200 trajectories ever got past it. More steps will not rescue a face with nothing to grip.
setting.harden_steps: Gradient steps in the stage that firms up a design that already looks like a binder. Rejections here mean something real was found and could not be made solid, which is a different problem from failing at anneal.
setting.mutate_steps: Gradient steps in the last polishing stage, where individual positions are changed. On a workable epitope this is where most of the attrition happens, because the design is good enough to be worth polishing and still has to clear the final bar.
setting.autotune: Lets BindCraft2 nudge the screen and refine stage lengths every ten trajectories, within safe bounds. It never touches recycles, the validation pool or the starting conformation. On by default and worth leaving on. Turning it off is part of what the benchmark profile does, for a run you can reproduce exactly.
setting.design_models: How many AlphaFold models drive the design stages. More models is a harder, slower target to satisfy and gives a design that fewer predictors disagree about. The design pool and the validation pool must not overlap, so raising this too far leaves nothing to validate with and the campaign is refused.
setting.validation_model: Which predictor judges a finished design, monomer or multimer. It is deliberately not one of the models used to design, so that validation is an independent opinion rather than a mark awarded by the same marker.
setting.design_recycles: How many times a prediction is fed back into itself during design. More recycles means a better prediction and a slower trajectory. The desperation ladder raises this on its last rung.
setting.validation_recycles: Recycles used when judging a finished design. Higher than design_recycles on purpose, because validation is run once per candidate and accuracy matters more than speed there.
setting.sequence_candidates: How many sequences ProteinMPNN writes for each accepted backbone. More candidates is a better chance that one of them folds and binds, at a refolding cost per candidate.
setting.enough_passing_sequences: Stop refolding this backbone once this many of its sequences have passed. It caps the work spent on a backbone that is clearly working, so the GPU moves on to the next trajectory.
setting.kept_sequences: How many passing sequences are kept per backbone in the ranked output. Raising it gives you more to order from one backbone, which is less diverse than the same number of designs from different backbones.
setting.mpnn_variant: Which ProteinMPNN weights redesign the sequence. The negative variant is trained to avoid the interface residues it should not touch. Changing this changes the character of every sequence the campaign produces.
setting.redesign_interface: Whether ProteinMPNN is allowed to rewrite the interface residues as well as the rest of the binder. Off keeps the contacts the trajectory found. On explores more sequence space and risks losing the interaction that made the backbone worth keeping.
setting.min_plddt_screen: The confidence floor a design must clear to survive screening. pLDDT is how sure the predictor is about the fold itself, not about binding. A low floor here lets vague early structures through to be refined.
setting.min_plddt_refine: The confidence floor at the refine stage. Raising the early floors kills attempts sooner and saves GPU time on a target that works, and on a hard target it can kill attempts that would have recovered.
setting.min_plddt_anneal: The confidence floor at anneal. Worth reading with min_iptm_anneal, because a design dropped here for pLDDT failed to fold, while one dropped for i_pTM folded and did not bind.
setting.min_plddt_harden: The confidence floor at harden. By this stage a design that cannot hold a confident fold is unlikely to become one.
setting.min_plddt_mutate: The confidence floor during the final polishing stage.
setting.min_plddt_final: The confidence floor a finished design has to clear to be accepted at all. This is the one that decides what lands in the ranked table.
setting.min_iptm_anneal: The interface confidence floor at anneal, and the single number that decides whether an epitope is workable. i_pTM is the predictor's confidence that the two chains are actually in contact. A value near 0.1 is the model saying there is no interface at all, which is what our Face B run produced throughout.
setting.min_iptm_harden: The interface confidence floor at harden. A design that has reached here has an interface, and this asks whether it is a convincing one.
setting.min_iptm_mutate: The interface confidence floor during polishing.
setting.min_iptm_final: The interface confidence a finished design must reach to be accepted. Lowering it will not rescue a bad epitope, because a failing face never reaches this filter in the first place.
setting.min_monomer_plddt_final: How confidently the binder has to fold on its own, with the target taken away. It catches a design that only looks like a protein while it is leaning on the target.
setting.min_hotspot_contact_final: The fraction of your named hotspots a finished design has to touch. It is what makes a directed campaign actually directed. It also costs yield, because a design that found a better grip just off your epitope is thrown away.
setting.max_trajectories: How many design attempts the campaign makes before it stops. Together with number_of_final_designs it decides when a run ends. For comparing two epitopes fairly this has to be the only stopping rule, otherwise the easier face stops early and the numbers are not comparable.
setting.number_of_final_designs: Stop once this many designs have been accepted. Set low, a campaign on a good target finishes early and tells you little about the rate. Set out of reach, max_trajectories becomes the only stopping rule and the accepted count becomes a yield you can compare.
setting.campaign_seed: The seed for the whole campaign. Fixing it makes a run reproducible, which is what the benchmark profile does. Two campaigns you want to compare should share it.
setting.project_folder: Where the run writes. It holds the trajectories, the refolded candidates, the ranked table and the campaign metadata. Pointing a new run at a populated folder is refused unless resume is on.
setting.trajectory_only: Run the gradient stages and stop, with no ProteinMPNN and no refolding. The budget defaults to 100 trajectories. This is the cheap way to ask whether an epitope is designable at all, because the answer shows in which stage attempts die, and that happens before any of the expensive back half.
setting.resume: Carry on in a folder that already holds output instead of refusing to start. Useful after a crash. It also means a settings change can land on top of trajectories made under the old settings, so a folder that mixes the two is hard to read afterwards.
setting.save_design_frames: Keep the structure at every sequence update, which is thousands of files. It is what makes trajectory playback possible, and it is off by default, so a run without it produces nothing to watch.
setting.save_design_animations: Write an animation of each trajectory. Off by default, and like the frames it has to be asked for before the run, not after.
setting.save_loss_plots: Write the loss curves for each trajectory, so you can see what the optimiser was fighting rather than only where it stopped.
setting.save_design_trajectory: Keep the structure the hallucination stage ended on, before ProteinMPNN rewrites the sequence. It is one file per design rather than thousands, and it lets you read what redesign made of the binder against what it was handed.
setting.relax_accepted_designs: Run a short relaxation on accepted designs before they are written. It cleans up small geometry problems and costs time per accepted design.
setting.humanize: Scores the designed sequence against a panel of common MHC anchor motifs and filters on MHC_Anchor_Score. It is a coarse presentation estimate over a fixed allele panel and it is in development. It does not establish that a design is non-immunogenic, so treat it as a proxy.
setting.protease_stable: Penalises predicted cleavage by trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase and pepsin, each blocked by a following proline, and separately penalises exposed loops and exposed termini, since proteases attack flexible exposed backbone. Four textbook proteases and a burial proxy are not a measurement of serum half life.
setting.disulfide_staple: Allows cysteine and rewards a disulfide whose geometry matches a real bond, around 3.8 angstroms with a minimum sequence separation, requiring at least one in the accepted design. It rewards plausible geometry rather than a verified bond, and a disulfide will not survive a reducing environment.
setting.mixed_topology: Removes the default reward for helix and requires sheet, capping helix at about half and asking for at least a fifth sheet. It steers away from the all helical bundles de novo design tends to produce. Beta rich folds are harder to design and predict, so expect a lower hit rate.
setting.termini_together: Pulls the two chain ends close together, within about 7 angstroms, for grafting, cyclisation or loop insertion. It is geometry only and says nothing about whether the intended construct will express or fold.
setting.termini_accessible: Angles both chain ends away from the target, so a tag, fusion partner or immobilisation chemistry can be attached without clashing into the interface. Geometry only, as above.
setting.initial_guess: The old name for hard_target. It re-predicts each redesigned candidate starting from the pose the trajectory folded, rather than from a blank slate, which helps AlphaFold converge on difficult motifs like extended loops and shallow interfaces. Because the predictor is handed something close to the answer, validation is slightly less independent and the false positive rate rises a little.
setting.bigbang: The old name for large_complex. It seeds the gradient design stages from the coordinates on hand rather than from the origin, which gives AlphaFold a foothold on large complexes above roughly 600 residues that it cannot build from nothing. Same trade as hard_target: easier convergence, slightly less independent validation.
setting.desperation: If the campaign has accepted nothing for desperation_trajectories attempts, it starts trading difficulty away to get any design at all, one rung every further 50 trajectories, up through hard_target, target_flexibility, multimer validation and more recycles. Every rung raises the expected false positive rate, because the design was accepted against an easier task and judged more loosely. The ladder is dropped the moment anything is accepted.
setting.desperation_trajectories: How many accepted-nothing trajectories go by before the desperation ladder starts. The default is 750. On a campaign shorter than that the ladder never runs, which is usually what you want when you are measuring whether an epitope works.
setting.design_dropout: Whether dropout is on in the predictor during the design stages. It adds noise, so trajectories explore more and repeat each other less, at the cost of a slightly noisier signal to optimise against.
setting.mpnn_model: Which ProteinMPNN checkpoint rewrites the sequence. Changing it changes the character of every sequence the campaign produces, so two campaigns you want to compare should use the same one.
setting.save_failed_trajectories: Keep the attempts that were rejected instead of discarding them. On by default, and worth leaving on, because on a failing epitope the rejected attempts are the entire result. Our Face B run produced no accepted designs at all, so without these there would have been nothing to look at.
setting.save_failed_refolds: Keep the refolded candidates that did not clear the filters. On by default. They are how you tell a backbone that no sequence could realise from one that was never worth redesigning.
setting.save_binder_monomers: Keep the prediction of the binder on its own, with the target taken away. On by default. It is what min_monomer_plddt_final is judged on, and it answers whether a design is a real protein or only looks like one while it leans on the target.
